extracted.intended_audience: novelists and memoirists preparing query letters to agents or editors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for composing query letters that persuade agents or editors to request a manuscript, focused mainly on novel (and memoir) fiction querying. Covers structure, wording, comps, bio, formatting, timing, and submission strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of the query letter
rubrics_metrics.description: The query letter has one purpose, and one purpose only: to seduce the agent or editor into reading or requesting your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the query as a sales piece; you can often write it without having written the manuscript, but you must have a firm grasp of your story premise and its appeal in today’s market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript readiness before querying
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelists and most memoirists should have a finished and polished manuscript before they begin querying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waiting avoids awkward situations if an agent responds quickly or the manuscript needs more work. “Wait until you feel the manuscript is totally done—the best you can make it.” You don't necessarily need to hire editors, but fix known problems first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall length and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: In its entirety, the query shouldn’t run more than 1 page, single spaced, or somewhere around 200 to 450 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity is recommended—especially if you lack confidence. “Get in, get out.” Avoid over-explaining, which can squeeze the life out of your story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housekeeping elements to include
rubrics_metrics.description: Include your book’s genre/category, word count, title/subtitle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These can be stated upfront or saved for the end of the query. If your word count is off-putting (e.g., >120,000 words), consider withholding it until the end after you’ve hooked the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story description length and centrality
rubrics_metrics.description: The story description is the most critical query element; 150–300 words is sufficient for most narrative works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For most queries the story description does most of the work. Focus on character and plot balance so the reader understands why they should care and what tension drives the story forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comp titles (comparable titles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comp titles are required by most agents and publishers; choose recent, meaningful comps that show where your book fits in the marketplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer titles released within a few years or authors who are actively publishing and whose readership aligns with your potential audience. Avoid international blockbusters turned movies (they don't offer meaningful comparisons) and avoid classic/dead authors. Sales figures and Amazon reviews matter less than critical reception and thoughtful alignment. Agents can help refine comps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bio note content and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a brief bio—usually 50–100 words—containing relevant publication credits and credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about publication credits; if you have no meaningful credits, don't invent them. Mention profession only if it lends credibility to the book, relevant research, significant awards (widely recognizable), and writing credentials (degrees, organizations). Self-published history is neutral unless accompanied by exceptional sales; if so, mention figures and ratings. Avoid irrelevant personal anecdotes or apologetic details. If unsure, leave out the bio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether to personalize the query
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization/customization of the query is optional but can help when meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful personalization should demonstrate specific knowledge about the agent/editor that can't be copied by others (e.g., referencing praise from an author the agent represents). Avoid boilerplate lines like 'I found you in Writer’s Market' or 'you represent mysteries' without added specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening the query effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with your strongest selling point: a referral, a conference request, or your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If vouched for or referred, mention that immediately. If you met at a conference and material was requested, put that up front. Starting with the story is a classic and preferred approach when you lack a meaningful personalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count norms and thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry standards: ~80,000 words typical for a debut novel; minimum generally 50,000; beyond 120,000 presents challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your word count is atypical, you may withhold it until later in the letter after you've hooked the reader. Consult genre-specific word count guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to compose the story description (core questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe who the protagonist is, what problem they face, the choices/tension that drive the story, what they want, why they want it, and what keeps them from getting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish setting/time immediately when necessary (e.g., historical or SF/F). Balance character and plot; highlight a unique twist or element to prevent the premise from sounding derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags in story descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs your description could be improved: runs longer than 300 words; reveals the ending (unless a specific agent preference); mentions more than three characters; includes minor plot points that don't affect the protagonist's choices; talks about the story instead of showing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep focus on what happens and the central tension. If an agent explicitly asks for ending information (Mary Kole’s note), follow that agent’s preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding tired or derivative ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-written description can still be boring if the idea feels done; your query should show an element that makes the work unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely in your genre to understand conventions and what’s been done. Add twists or uncommon conflicts to make familiar elements compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: What not to include in a query
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude irrelevant personal details and certain appeals: years of effort, how much family/friends love your work, number of rejections or close accepts, money invested in editing, and vague praises from unnamed readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a well-known mentor or author will blurb the book, mention that. Avoid apologizing or begging; be professional and concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market concerns and marketing plan (novel-specific guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel queries don’t have to address audience, marketing plan, or platform; you sell the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memoir and nonfiction differ; save market/readership details for a book proposal unless you have an exceptional platform (e.g., 100,000+ fans) in which case mention it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closing the query professionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Close with a thank-you, sign your name, and include contact info (email, maybe phone) at the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't state availability for in-person meetings or insist on exclusivity unless guidelines demand. Mention a planned series briefly if relevant. Resist editorializing about the book's greatness or pleading for attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission strategy / batching
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize agents into rounds or buckets (A list, B list, everyone else) and submit in waves (5–10 at a time) including a mix of agent types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an A-list agent responds favorably early, send another mixed round to generate competing interest. If responses indicate a pattern of problems, adjust your approach in the next round. Conservative staged submission is easier psychologically but bulk submissions are also acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for queries
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no universally ‘good’ or ‘bad’ time to query; if the agent/publisher accepts submissions and your material is ready, submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-analyzing calendar timing (e.g., August/holidays) since agents' availability varies. The author offers an opinionated month-by-month chance list if readers insist on timing guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email-specific formatting and etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: For email queries: strip formatting, send as plain text in block style, no address or date headers at the top; put contact info at the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First line should read 'Dear [Agent Name]:'; use shorter paragraphs and paragraph breaks for email readability; follow any agent-specific rules even if you disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to handle responses and exclusives
rubrics_metrics.description: If you don’t hear back, assume it’s a rejection and move on. If an agent asks for an exclusive read, be cautious; don’t grant lengthy exclusives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend exclusive periods be short (maybe ~2 weeks). If a second agent requests while the manuscript is under consideration, inform them it’s under consideration elsewhere. If a second agent offers representation first, inform the first and give them a chance to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and concise formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short, well-crafted example sentences and formulas (one-sentence descriptions from PublishersMarketplace) to learn what excites agents and to practice succinct pitching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study recent sales and one-sentence deal descriptions to see current trends and how to position your book in a few words.
